title: Integrated Causal Reasoning Assessment: Two Communities
description: Assesses student understanding of group-level cooperation, composition effects, and the tension between individual and collective interests.

vignette.title: The Two Villages
vignette.text:
Two neighboring villages, Green Valley and Blue Hill, each have 20 families who share a common forest. In Green Valley, 15 families are modest (harvest sustainably) and 5 are greedy (harvest too much). In Blue Hill, 10 families are modest and 10 are greedy.

Both villages have the same forest size and regrowth rate. Over several years, the villages have different outcomes. Green Valley's forest remains healthy, while Blue Hill's forest becomes depleted.

A new student, Alex, looks at the situation and says: 'The problem is that Blue Hill has more greedy families. If they just had more modest families like Green Valley, everything would be fine.'

items.question: Based on the model, why does Green Valley have better outcomes than Blue Hill?

options.text: Green Valley has better people who care more about the environment.
options.misconception: Individual-blame framing that ignores systemic structure and composition effects.

options.text: Green Valley has a higher proportion of modest families, which creates a different collective outcome even though individual behavior is the same.
options.explanation: Recognizes that group composition affects collective outcomes, not just individual character. The same individual behaviors can lead to different group-level results depending on proportions.

options.text: Green Valley's forest regrows faster than Blue Hill's forest.
options.misconception: Assumes ecological differences when the problem is social structure.

options.text: The modest families in Green Valley are more effective at convincing greedy families to change their behavior.
options.misconception: Assumes persuasion rather than structural effects.

items.competencyTarget: Understanding composition effects and collective outcomes

items.question: If Blue Hill wanted to improve their forest outcomes, what would be most effective?

options.text: Punish the greedy families more severely to make them change their behavior.
options.misconception: Punishment-focused solution that ignores composition effects and may not address root causes.

options.text: Educate the greedy families about why their behavior is harmful.
options.misconception: Education-focused solution that assumes individual behavior change without addressing structural incentives.

options.text: Increase the proportion of modest families in the community, which would change the collective dynamics.
options.explanation: Recognizes that changing group composition affects collective outcomes, even if individual behaviors remain the same.

options.text: Build a fence around the forest to prevent greedy families from harvesting.
options.misconception: External authority solution that doesn't address the underlying social dynamics.

items.question: A student says: 'If we just had all modest families, there would be no problem.' What is the most accurate response?

options.text: The student is right - all modest families would solve the problem completely.
options.misconception: Assumes a simple solution without considering whether all-modest is stable or realistic.

options.text: The student is wrong - even all modest families would eventually become greedy because of human nature.
options.misconception: Genetic determinism that assumes fixed human nature.

options.text: While all modest families would lead to good outcomes, this may not be stable if modest families have lower individual benefits than greedy families.
options.explanation: Recognizes that even if a state is desirable, it may not be stable if there are incentives to defect. The question is about stability, not just desirability.

options.text: The composition of families doesn't matter - only the total number of families matters.

items.question: How does the Two Communities model differ from the Two Foresters model in what it shows about cooperation?

options.text: Two Communities shows that cooperation is impossible, while Two Foresters shows it's possible.
options.misconception: False dichotomy that ignores the role of conditions and parameters.

options.text: Two Communities shows group-level effects, while Two Foresters shows individual-level effects.
options.explanation: Recognizes that Two Communities adds the dimension of group composition and collective outcomes, while Two Foresters focuses on individual interaction.

options.text: Two Communities is more realistic because it has more agents.
options.misconception: Assumes more agents = more realistic, ignoring the conceptual difference.

options.text: There's no real difference - they show the same thing.
options.misconception: Ignores the conceptual difference between individual and group-level dynamics.

items.question: If we added a third community with 18 modest families and 2 greedy families, what would we expect to happen?

options.text: This community would have the best outcomes because it has the most modest families.
options.misconception: Assumes linear relationship without considering diminishing returns or other factors.

options.text: This community would have worse outcomes because the 2 greedy families would take advantage of the modest families.
options.misconception: Assumes greedy families always undermine cooperation, ignoring composition effects.

options.text: This community would likely have good outcomes, possibly better than Green Valley, due to the high proportion of modest families.
options.explanation: Recognizes that higher proportions of modest families generally lead to better collective outcomes, though the relationship may not be perfectly linear.

options.text: We can't predict anything without knowing more about the individual families.
options.misconception: Individual-focused thinking that ignores the power of composition effects.

integratedReasoning.description: Student recognizes group-level effects, composition effects, and the difference between individual and collective outcomes.
indicators: Understands how group composition affects collective outcomes
Can make predictions based on composition

dichotomizedReasoning.description: Student relies on individual-blame explanations, assumes simple linear relationships, or ignores group-level dynamics.
indicators: Frames problems in terms of individual character
Assumes simple solutions without considering stability

commonMisconceptions: Individual blame: Attributing outcomes to character rather than composition
Simple solutions: Assuming one factor will solve everything
Ignoring stability: Not considering whether outcomes are stable
Linear thinking: Assuming simple proportional relationships
suggestedActivities: Run the model with different group compositions and observe outcomes
Compare Two Communities with Two Foresters to understand different levels of analysis
Discuss real-world examples of composition effects (classrooms, teams, communities)
Use causal mapping to diagram how composition affects outcomes
